## Agenda {.agenda}

1. Use the command line to navigate a project and run programs
2. Use Git to record and recover project states
3. Use Git while building an individual research project
4. Record the inputs, environment, and commands needed to reproduce a result

::: {.notes}
The lecture has two connected layers. Git records project history. Reproducible
research requires enough information to run a selected version again.

The command line is supporting material. Teach only the concepts needed to
understand the Git examples and scripted research workflows.

Suggested timing: command line, 10 minutes; Git concepts and exercises,
30 minutes; building a reproducible project, 35 minutes; recap, 5 minutes.
:::

## Command line interface {.section-divider}

## A terminal lets you navigate files and run programs

- On macOS: **Terminal** or an installed application such as **iTerm2**
- On Windows: **PowerShell**, **Windows Terminal**, or **Git Bash**
- In an editor: an integrated terminal, such as the terminal in VS Code

```text
current folder → enter a command → a program runs → text output
```

::: {.notes}
The terminal is an application that displays the command-line interface. A
shell reads each command and starts the requested program. Students do not
need to memorize that distinction today.

The current folder provides context. A student can inspect files, move between
folders, and run a program that reads or writes files in that project.

Source: [Missing Semester: Course Overview and the Shell](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/course-shell/).
:::

## Structure of a command

```bash
ls -la data/
python code/clean.py data/raw/survey.csv
git log --oneline
```

| Example | Program | Subcommand | Option | Argument |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ls -la data/` | `ls` | — | `-la` | `data/` |
| `python code/clean.py data/raw/survey.csv` | `python` | — | — | script and input file |
| `git log --oneline` | `git` | `log` | `--oneline` | — |

::: {.notes}
An argument supplies an input to a program. An option or flag changes the
program's behavior. Command structure differs across programs, so use
`<command> --help` or documentation when needed.

Students do not need to memorize every command. They need to read a command,
identify its parts, and verify its effect.

Source: [Missing Semester: Command-line Environment](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/command-line-environment/).
:::

## A small command-line vocabulary

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| Show the current directory | `pwd` |
| List files | `ls` |
| Change directory | `cd <path>` |
| Create a directory | `mkdir <path>` |
| Read a text file | `cat <file>` |
| Find the executable for a program | `which <program>` |
| Show an installed program's version | `<program> --version` |
| Get help | `<command> --help` |

::: {.notes}
These examples use a Unix-style shell on macOS or Linux. Windows PowerShell
has related commands, but some syntax differs. Git concepts do not depend on
the shell.

`which` is a Unix command. In PowerShell, use `Get-Command <program>`. The
`--version` and `--help` options are common conventions, but a program can use
different options. Check its documentation when either option fails.

Do not turn this section into a syntax survey. The core ideas are programs,
arguments, options, paths, and observable output.
:::

## Git's data model {.section-divider}

::: {.notes}
Students already created and cloned their course repository and completed the
pre-class Git workflow. Use this section to explain what each command changed.
Do not repeat the assignment as a syntax demonstration.
:::

## Organization without version control

```text
analysis.py
analysis_new.py
analysis_final.py
analysis_final_fixed.py
analysis_final_final_no_seriously.py
analysis_final_final_2026-09-22.py
```

::: {.notes}
The filenames record guesses about importance, not a reliable history. Copies
also hide which lines changed and why.

The problem is not only untidy filenames. The researcher cannot connect a
result to a specific state of the complete project.
:::

## Version control records project states

```text
●  Add a quadratic age term to analysis.py
│
●  Correct the treatment variable in analysis.py
│
●  Create the initial analysis.py
```

Each **commit** records a project snapshot and an explanation.

::: {.notes}
Define a commit as a recorded project snapshot plus metadata. The metadata
include its parent, author, time, and message.

Git stores file differences efficiently. Think of its history as a sequence
or graph of complete project states.
:::

## Git records history and GitHub stores a remote copy

```text
Your computer                         GitHub
Git + local repository  ←────────→   remote Git repository
                                      + website and collaboration tools
```

- **Git** is the version-control software
- **GitHub uses Git** to store another copy of the repository
- Git works locally without GitHub or an internet connection

::: {.notes}
A local repository contains its own history. GitHub hosts a remote Git
repository and adds a website, access controls, issues, and pull requests.

Students will use GitHub in the course, but GitHub is not the version-control
system.
:::

## A Git repository contains a graph

<div class="commit-graph linear">
<div class="commit"><span>C1</span><small>Baseline code</small></div>
<div class="arrow">←</div>
<div class="commit"><span>C2</span><small>Treatment variable fixed</small></div>
<div class="arrow">←</div>
<div class="commit current"><span>C3</span><small>Quadratic term added</small></div>
</div>

- Each commit records a snapshot
- Each commit identifies its parent
- The history records relationships, not only dates

Each circle represents a recorded state of the project.

::: {.notes}
The arrows point from a commit to its parent. Git history is a directed acyclic
graph. Students do not need that term, but they should understand that history
can branch and later merge.

The commit identifier is derived from content. Short labels such as C1 are for
teaching only. Git uses hashes.

Source: [Missing Semester: Version Control and Git](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/version-control/).
:::

## A commit is more than a saved file

```text
commit 8e12c4a
Parent:  47d906b
Author:  Student Name
Date:    2026-09-16

    Correct treatment coding
```

Best practice: make each commit one coherent change that you can explain in one sentence.

::: {.notes}
The snapshot covers the repository, not only one file. The parent connects the
snapshot to history. The message records intent.

Recommend small commits that leave the project in a coherent state. A commit
should be large enough to represent one meaningful change and small enough to
explain in one sentence.
:::

## Commits stay local until you push them

<div class="state-zones"><span>On your computer</span><span>On GitHub</span></div>

<div class="state-flow">
<div><strong>Working tree</strong><small>Files you edit</small></div>
<div class="flow-arrow">→<code>git add</code>→</div>
<div><strong>Staging area</strong><small>Proposed snapshot</small></div>
<div class="flow-arrow">→<code>git commit</code>→</div>
<div><strong>Local repository</strong><small>Commits on your computer</small></div>
<div class="flow-arrow">→<code>git push</code>→</div>
<div><strong>Remote repository</strong><small>Commits on GitHub</small></div>
</div>

`git pull` brings remote commits into the current local branch and updates the working files.

::: {.notes}
The working tree and staging area are local. `git add` selects content for the
next commit. `git commit` records that snapshot in the local repository.

Only `git push` sends commits to the remote repository. A commit can exist on
the student's computer without existing on GitHub.

`git pull` combines two operations: fetch remote commits, then integrate them
into the current branch. This explains why pulling can change working files.
:::

## Exercise: which version will Git commit?

```bash
# The last commit contains the old model
# The working file now contains model A
git add analysis.py

# Edit the working file again. It now contains model B
git commit -m "Estimate baseline model"
```

| Location | Content before `git commit` |
|---|---|
| Last commit | Old model |
| Staging area | Model A |
| Working file | Model B |

Which model will the new commit contain? What happens to the other two versions?

::: {.notes}
Answer: the new commit contains Model A. Model B remains in the working file.
The old model remains available through the parent commit.

`git add` copies the selected content into the staging area. A later edit to
the working file does not update the staged copy. Run `git add` again if the
later edit belongs in the commit.
:::

## The correct undo command depends on the state

| Where is the unwanted change? | Goal | Command model |
|---|---|---|
| Working file only | Discard the local edit | `git restore <file>` |
| Staging area | Remove it from the proposed commit and keep the edit | `git restore --staged <file>` |
| A commit others might have | Preserve history and reverse its effect | `git revert <commit>` |

First locate the change. Then choose how Git should handle it.

::: {.notes}
The same word, “undo,” describes different operations. Students should first
ask whether the change is only in a working file, staged, committed locally,
or already pushed.

`git revert` creates a new commit. It is the safe default for reversing a
commit that another copy of the repository might contain. Do not introduce
history-rewriting commands as the default recovery method.
:::

## A branch is a movable name for a commit

<svg class="branch-map" viewBox="0 0 1100 330" role="img" aria-label="Commit graph with main and alternative-specification branches">
  <line x1="100" y1="120" x2="530" y2="120" />
  <line x1="300" y1="120" x2="500" y2="245" />
  <line x1="500" y1="245" x2="700" y2="245" />
  <circle cx="100" cy="120" r="34" /><circle cx="300" cy="120" r="34" />
  <circle cx="530" cy="120" r="34" /><circle cx="500" cy="245" r="34" />
  <circle cx="700" cy="245" r="34" class="current-node" />
  <text x="100" y="130">C1</text><text x="300" y="130">C2</text>
  <text x="530" y="130">C3</text><text x="500" y="255">C4</text>
  <text x="700" y="255">C5</text>
  <text x="590" y="130" class="branch-name">main</text>
  <text x="750" y="238" class="branch-name alt-name">alternative-specification</text>
  <text x="750" y="274" class="head-name">HEAD</text>
</svg>

`main` points to C3; `alternative-specification` points to C5. `HEAD` identifies the current branch.

::: {.notes}
A branch is a movable name, not a copy of the project directory. Each new
commit advances the current branch name. Both branches retain their shared
history before the split.

Switching branches changes which recorded project state appears in the working
tree. It does not delete the other line of work.
:::

## Exercise: follow HEAD after a commit

```bash
# Start on main at commit C3
git switch main
git switch -c alternative-specification
# edit analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Estimate quadratic specification"
```

Think about the project immediately after the commit:

- Which commit does `HEAD` identify?
- Which version of `analysis.py` appears if you switch to `main`?
- Does switching to `main` delete the new commit?

::: {.notes}
Answers: `HEAD` identifies the new commit on `alternative-specification`.
Switching to `main` restores the version from C3. The new commit remains
available through the `alternative-specification` label.

The value of the question is reasoning about the graph, not command
memorization. Students who can reason about the graph can usually recover from
an unfamiliar situation.
:::

## A research decision determines what happens to a branch

| Decision | Use it when... |
|---|---|
| **Merge** | The branch's changes should become part of `main` |
| **Retain for now** | The decision is pending and the work is worth revisiting |
| **Delete** | The work is rejected and the branch name no longer provides value |

If an alternative matters to the paper, preserve its code and result on `main` even when it is not the preferred specification.

::: {.notes}
Merging is a research decision, not the automatic end of every branch. A
researcher can retain a branch when the alternative and its history remain
informative.

Record consequential alternatives in the paper or research log. Delete
short-lived branches after their work is merged or the separate label has no
further value. `git branch -d` refuses to
delete an unmerged branch. Git does not delete a merged commit when it deletes
the redundant branch label.
:::

## A fast-forward merge moves the current branch label

```text
Before merge

C1 ← C2 ← C3             main (HEAD)
          ↖ C4           alternative-specification

git switch main                    # destination
git merge alternative-specification

After merge

C1 ← C2 ← C3 ← C4
                  ├── main (HEAD)
                  └── alternative-specification
```

Git moves `main` to C4 without creating a merge commit. The source branch still points to C4.

::: {.notes}
`git merge alternative-specification` integrates that branch into the current
branch. The command does not mean “merge main into alternative-specification.”
The current branch is the destination.

The merge does not blindly overwrite the destination. In this example, the
source branch began at `main` and contains all of its earlier work. The source branch label remains after the merge and can be deleted once
its separate name is no longer useful.
:::

## Exercise: can Git fast-forward this merge?

```text
C1 ← C2 ← C3 ← C5        main (HEAD)
          ↖ C4           alternative-specification
```

You run `git merge alternative-specification`.

- Can Git move `main` directly to C4?
- Why might Git need a merge commit?
- When could Git ask you to resolve a conflict?

::: {.notes}
Answers: Git cannot fast-forward because `main` and the alternative branch both
advanced after C3. Git must combine the two histories, usually with a merge
commit. A conflict can occur if C4 and C5 changed the same lines or made other
changes that Git cannot combine automatically.
:::

## A divergent merge combines two lines of work

```text
Before merge

             C5  main (HEAD)
            ↗
C1 ← C2 ← C3
            ↘
             C4  alternative-specification

After merge

             C5 ───────┐
            ↗          ↓
C1 ← C2 ← C3           C6  main (HEAD)
            ↘          ↑
             C4 ───────┘   alternative-specification stays at C4
```

C6 records the combined result. It has C5 and C4 as parents.

::: {.notes}
`git merge alternative-specification` runs while `main` is current. Git
combines changes made since the shared ancestor C3. The merge commit C6
preserves both lines of history. The source branch name still identifies C4.

If the branches changed unrelated parts of the project, Git can often combine
them automatically. If their changes disagree, a person must resolve the
conflict before C6 can be recorded.
:::

## A merge conflict marks a decision Git cannot make

```text
Shared starting line:  weight = baseline_weight

main changes it to:   weight = revised_baseline_weight
branch changes it to: weight = alternative_weight
```

Git pauses the merge and marks the conflicting lines in the file.

```text
Inspect both versions → choose the intended code
Run checks → stage the resolved file → commit the merge
```

The result may keep one version, both versions, or a new solution.

::: {.notes}
Conflicts are not evidence that either branch is wrong. Git cannot infer which
research specification should be primary. It identifies the overlapping
changes and asks the researcher to write the intended result.

Show conflict markers if students ask, but make the decision model central.
After editing the file, run the relevant analysis or tests, stage the resolved
file, and finish the merge commit. Do not automatically accept "ours" or
"theirs" without understanding the content.
:::

## Exercise: integrate a robustness check without replacing the baseline

```text
main:        baseline weights → primary estimate
alternative: replaces weights → different estimate
decision:    keep primary, report alternative as a check
```

- Would merging the branch as written preserve both estimates?
- What should the code produce before you merge it into `main`?
- What should the research record say about the difference?

::: {.notes}
The source branch currently replaces the baseline calculation. An automatic
merge could leave only the alternative version, especially if `main` has not
changed since the branch point. Revise the branch so one scripted workflow
computes both estimates and labels them clearly. Run it and compare outputs.
Then merge the revised branch into `main`. Document the size of the change and
the reason the baseline weights remain primary. This is a substantive
research decision, not a Git conflict resolution rule.
:::

## Remote commands move commits between repositories

| Command | Mental model |
|---|---|
| `git clone <url>` | Create a local repository and connect it to the remote |
| `git fetch` | Update your local view of remote commits without changing your working files |
| `git pull --ff-only` | Fetch, then move your current branch forward only when no histories must be combined |
| `git push` | Send local commits and advance the corresponding remote branch |

::: {.notes}
Cloning is usually a one-time setup action. Fetch, pull, and push synchronize
repositories. They do not synchronize one shared live folder.

The pre-class exercise used `git pull --ff-only`. The option refuses the pull
when local and remote histories have diverged. It prevents Git from choosing a
merge strategy before the student understands the situation.
:::

## Exercise: predict what these remote commands do

```text
             C4  main (remote)   (README edit)
            ↗
C1 ← C2 ← C3
            ↘
             C5  main (local)    (analysis commit)
```

Predict the result of each command:

1. Does `git push origin main` move remote `main` to C5, or does Git reject it? Explain from the graph.
2. Does `git pull --ff-only origin main` move local `main` to include C4, or does it stop? Explain from the graph.
3. After `git fetch origin`, does `origin/main` move? Do the project files change? What can `git log --oneline --graph --all` show?

::: {.notes}
`git push` is rejected because the remote `main` has C4, which the local branch
does not contain. Accepting C5 as the new remote tip would make C4 no longer
reachable from `main`. `git pull --ff-only` also stops because neither branch
is an ancestor of the other. `git fetch` updates the local record of the remote
tracking branch but does not change the project files. The log command lets
students inspect both lines of history. After inspection, they can choose a
merge or another integration method, resolve any conflicts, and push the result.
:::

## Build a reproducible research project {.section-divider}

## What must accompany a result?

- The code version: identify the Git commit
- The input data: identify the exact files or release
- The environment and settings: record what the code needs
- The run command and expected output: show how to recreate the result

::: {.notes}
A repository can preserve the analysis code while omitting the data, package
versions, seed, or run instructions. Your future self may face the same gaps
as another researcher.
:::

## Exercise: what could make results fail to replicate?

Two researchers check out the same commit. Each has a copy of the input data.

<div class="comparison">
<div>
<h3>Scenario 1: cannot run</h3>
<p>The script stops before producing a result.</p>
<p>Name two plausible explanations.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h3>Scenario 2: different result</h3>
<p>The script runs, but the estimate differs.</p>
<p>Name two plausible explanations.</p>
</div>
</div>

For each scenario, identify what you would record or change to prevent it.

::: {.notes}
Do not cue students with a software-version example. Let them identify the
missing dimensions. A can result from an absolute path, missing package,
missing credential, or unavailable external service. B can result from a
different data snapshot, random draw, package version, numerical library,
time-dependent query, or language-model response. Some conditions can cause
either outcome. Ask which problems prevent execution and which let the code
run but change its output.
:::

## Start with the course repository

```text
Course template → your GitHub repository → clone → your computer
```

```text
fa26-1433-YOUR-KERBEROS/
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── code/
├── data/
└── output/
```

```bash
git clone https://github.com/YOU/fa26-1433-YOUR-KERBEROS.git
```

::: {.notes}
Students first created a repository from the course template on GitHub. The
template supplied the starting directory structure and documentation. Their
new repository is separate from the template repository.

`git clone` then created the local directory, downloaded the files and commit
history, and recorded the GitHub repository as the remote named `origin`.
:::

## Store raw data according to access and size

| Data | Git practice |
|---|---|
| Restricted or confidential | Keep out of Git |
| Large | Store elsewhere and record its source and version |
| Small, non-sensitive, and immutable | Commit only if sharing is permitted |

Commit extraction code. Store excluded data in an approved location and document its exact version.

Use `.gitignore` for raw data that must stay outside Git.

::: {.notes}
Raw data must remain unchanged after acquisition. Cleaning scripts should read
the raw snapshot and write new derived files.

For data stored outside Git, record enough information to identify the exact
input. Depending on the source, this can include a release number, retrieval
date, URL, query, file name, and checksum.

Keep a second copy in approved institutional or cloud storage. A synced
folder helps protect against laptop loss, but does not identify a data
version. Confirm that the storage service is allowed before placing
restricted data there.

Git retains earlier versions of a committed file. Never commit restricted data,
secrets, or direct identifiers. Large binary data also make clones slow. Use an
approved data archive or storage service. Use Git LFS only when the project has
chosen and documented that workflow.

Sources: [GitHub repository limits](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/repository-limits) and [GitHub: Removing sensitive data](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/removing-sensitive-data-from-a-repository).
:::

## `.gitignore` keeps selected local files out of commits

**Contents of `.gitignore`:**

```text
# Restricted or large raw data
data/raw/

# Local environments and system files
.venv/
.DS_Store
```

- Commit `.gitignore` so every clone uses the same rules
- Add an ignore rule before you stage the file
- An ignore rule does not remove a file that Git already tracks

::: {.notes}
A `.gitignore` file specifies intentionally untracked files. It helps keep
generated files, local environments, and unsuitable data out of routine Git
operations.

An ignore rule is not an access-control or security mechanism. Never place a
secret or restricted file in Git history. Deleting it in a later commit does
not remove it from earlier commits.

Source: [Git documentation: gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore).
:::

## Check the project state before recording work

```text
$ git status

Untracked files:
  notes/research-question.md

Changes not staged for commit:
  modified: code/analyze.py

Changes to be committed:
  modified: README.md
```

- **Untracked:** exists in the folder but not in a commit or the staging area
- **Modified, not staged:** working file differs from the staged version
- **Staged:** selected for the next commit

::: {.notes}
Git observes files inside the working tree, but it records only the content
that the user stages and commits. An untracked file is a normal local file.
Git does not include it in a commit until the user stages it.

The short form, `git status --short`, uses `??` for untracked, ` M` for
modified but unstaged, and `M ` for staged. Use the full status output when
an abbreviation is unclear.
:::

## Record a coherent project change

```bash
git status
git add README.md code/analyze.py
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Add baseline analysis"
```

Review the staged diff before committing. The message completes: **This commit will...**

::: {.notes}
Do not recommend `git add .` as the only starting habit. Explicit paths make
the selection visible. `git add .` can be appropriate after the researcher
has inspected the complete status and ignore rules.

An imperative message such as “Add baseline analysis” states what the
commit does when applied.
:::

## Trace a result back to a code change

```bash
$ git log --oneline --decorate
3cb418f (HEAD -> main) Add baseline analysis
```

```text
Result:  Table 1 baseline estimate
Code:    commit 3cb418f
Data:    survey release 2026-09, crosswalk version 2
Run:     bash run.sh from the project root
Output:  output/estimates.csv
```

Record the commit ID with each important result; identify data separately.

::: {.notes}
This example applies Git's commit model to a research result. The commit ID
identifies the code and documentation in Git; it does not identify raw data
stored elsewhere. A data release, retrieval record, or checksum can identify
the exact external input. `git show 3cb418f` displays the recorded code
change. `git log --oneline -- code/analyze.py` traces one file's history.

The persistent log is one of Git's principal benefits for independent work.
It replaces memory and filename conventions with inspectable evidence. The
result record can live in a research log or result manifest.
:::

## Exercise: predict what happens when you switch branches

```text
alternative-specification
  committed version: C4
  working file: edits made after C4, not yet committed

main
  committed version: C2, with a different version of code/analyze.py
```

You want to inspect the committed version on `main`, then return to the edits.
What might happen to the working file when you switch branches?

::: {.notes}
Ask students to predict whether Git will switch branches, overwrite the
uncommitted edits, or stop. Git stops when switching would lose local edits. It can switch when the
changes do not conflict with the target branch. The point is to predict the interaction between
the committed version and the current working file before running a command.
:::

## `git stash` pauses edits without advancing the branch

<div class="stash-flow">
  <div><strong>1. Save</strong><code>git stash push</code><span>Git records the local edits in a stash</span></div>
  <div><strong>2. Switch</strong><code>git switch main</code><span>The working tree can show the committed files from main</span></div>
  <div><strong>3. Return</strong><code>git switch alternative-specification</code><span>Go back to the work branch</span></div>
  <div><strong>4. Restore</strong><code>git stash pop</code><span>Reapply the edits on that branch</span></div>
</div>

A stash is local and temporary. Apply it after returning to the branch where you paused.

By default, a stash does not include untracked files.

::: {.notes}
`git stash push` saves tracked working-tree and staged changes, then restores a
clean working tree. Git stores the stash internally, but the current branch
does not advance. `git stash pop` reapplies the most recent stash and removes
it from the stash list if it applies cleanly. Return to the original branch
first so the edits resume in their original context. A stash is not pushed.

Prefer a coherent commit when the work represents a project state worth
recording. Use a stash for a short interruption when the work is not ready to
commit.

Sources: [Git switch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-switch) and
[Git stash](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-stash).
:::

## Exercise: switch branches without losing unfinished work

```text
Current branch: alternative-specification
Tracked file:   code/analyze.py has uncommitted edits
New file:       notes/weighting.md has never been staged
Goal:           run the committed version on main, then resume both files
```

- Would a default `git stash push` save both files?
- How can you preserve both files before switching branches?
- Why might a checkpoint commit be better if this work is already coherent?

::: {.notes}
Answer: a default stash saves changes to tracked files, but not the new
`notes/weighting.md`. First inspect `git status`. Use `git stash push -u -m
"Pause alternative specification"` to include untracked files, switch to
`main`, then switch back and run `git stash pop`. The `-u` option includes
untracked files. Check status after restoring the stash.

A coherent checkpoint commit is another option when the work is in a state
worth recording. Do not create a misleading commit only to clear the working
tree.
:::

## If you need a Python notebook, choose marimo

A **notebook** lets you run code in cells beside notes, figures, and results.

| | Jupyter | marimo |
|---|---|---|
| Saved file | `.ipynb` JSON with code, metadata, and often outputs | A plain `.py` file |
| Git and coding agents | Changes can be harder to review and edit | Ordinary Python text is easier to diff and edit |
| Running cells | Old values can remain in memory | Dependent cells update or are marked stale |

**Course recommendation:** use marimo for new interactive Python work.

```bash
marimo edit notebooks/analysis.py  # explore
python notebooks/analysis.py       # rerun from the command line
```

::: {.notes}
This is a choice for students who want an interactive Python document. They
do not need to use a notebook at all. A Jupyter notebook is an `.ipynb` file
that stores cells, metadata, and outputs as JSON. That format can create noisy
Git diffs, and its interactive execution can leave values in memory that no
longer match the visible order of cells. Jupyter files can still be versioned
and executed from a command; do not imply otherwise.

marimo stores notebooks as Python source files. That makes code changes easier
to inspect in Git and gives a text-editing coding agent an ordinary Python
file to work with. Its reactive execution reruns affected cells or marks them
stale. A marimo notebook can also run as a script with `python notebook.py`.
The recommendation is for new Python notebook work, not a demand to convert
an existing Jupyter project or to replace simple scripts. Keep dependencies
in the project's environment recipe, and check data permissions before
committing any generated output.

Sources: [Jupyter notebook format](https://docs.jupyter.org/en/latest/reference/mimetype.html),
[marimo overview](https://docs.marimo.io/), and
[marimo project guidance](https://docs.marimo.io/guides/package_management/projects/).
:::

## Script each stage and run it from one entry point

<div class="pipeline">
<div class="optional-step">Extraction script(s)<small>optional step 0</small></div><span>→</span><div>Raw-data snapshot</div><span>→</span><div>Cleaning script(s)</div><span>→</span><div>Analysis script(s)</div><span>→</span><div>Results</div>
</div>

The workflow should have one documented entry point that runs the stages in order.

::: {.notes}
The entry point runs the stages in order. A reader should not need to infer
an undocumented manual step between boxes. The extraction step is optional
when a raw-data snapshot is already available. The snapshot preserves the
inputs used for one result even if the external source later changes.

If the data source provides a stable download rather than an API, step 0 can
be a documented download command or procedure.
:::

## Use project-relative paths so the workflow can run elsewhere

```python
import pandas as pd

# Run the project command from the repository root.
data = pd.read_csv("data/raw/survey.csv")
```

A relative path works when the run command starts from the documented project root.

::: {.notes}
The portable example assumes a defined project root. The run instructions
must state where to execute the command, or the code should determine the root
reliably.

Also document file names, encodings, expected columns, and access restrictions
when these details affect the run.
:::

## A shell script records command order

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
python code/extract.py    # writes data/raw/survey.csv
python code/clean.py      # reads survey and crosswalk; writes data/clean.csv
Rscript code/estimate.R   # writes output/estimates.csv
```

Run this from the project root. The script stops if a command fails.

::: {.notes}
This shell script is a concrete entry point for the workflow above. Shell
scripts can run several programs in sequence. The comments describe inputs and
outputs for a person. The shell does not use those comments to decide which
commands to run. Each successful run executes every listed command. `set -e`
stops after a failed command, while `-u` catches unset variables and
`pipefail` catches failures inside pipelines. This example assumes Bash is
available. The crosswalk is a separately supplied raw input.
:::

## Exercise: how could you avoid rerunning every command?

Use the script on the previous slide.

1. You changed only `estimate.R`. Which outputs are still valid and can be reused?
2. `crosswalk.csv` changed, but neither script changed. What must be rebuilt before you trust `estimates.csv`?
3. What file relationships would an automation tool need to know to make these decisions?

::: {.notes}
When only `estimate.R` changes, `clean.csv` can be reused and only the final
estimate must be rebuilt. When `crosswalk.csv` changes, the cleaning step must
rebuild `clean.csv` before estimation. Running only the last command in the
second case could produce a plausible estimate from stale cleaned data. To
choose the right commands, automation must know which files each step reads
and writes. This information forms a dependency graph.
:::

## Make records dependencies between inputs and outputs

| Output | Required inputs |
|---|---|
| `data/clean.csv` | `data/raw/survey.csv`, `data/raw/crosswalk.csv`, `code/clean.py` |
| `output/estimates.csv` | `data/clean.csv`, `code/estimate.R` |

Make can use declared file dependencies and modification times to decide what to rerun.

::: {.notes}
The first rule must list both raw data files and the cleaning script as
prerequisites. The second must list the cleaned data and estimation script.
If only `estimate.R` changes, Make can rerun estimation. If a raw input
changes, it can rerun cleaning and then estimation. Make compares file
modification times, so it only works as intended when the declared
dependencies are complete. The extraction step needs its own rule or a
separate documented command when raw data must be regenerated.

Source: [GNU Make manual: prerequisites](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Prerequisite-Types.html).
:::

## Three ways to automate project steps

| Option | What it runs | How it decides what to run |
|---|---|---|
| One Python script | Python analysis steps | Runs the steps written in the script, in order |
| Shell script | Commands from Python and other command-line programs | Runs the listed commands, in order |
| Makefile | Commands from Python and other command-line programs | Rebuilds targets with newer declared prerequisites |

::: {.notes}
One Python script is simple when all steps use Python. It becomes awkward when
it must coordinate other applications. A shell script is a file of terminal
commands. It can run Python, R, and other command-line programs in sequence.
A Makefile can run those same commands. It also records a dependency graph,
such as which data and scripts produce each output. Make uses that graph to
rerun the steps affected by a change and leave other outputs alone. Make can
only do this when the dependency rules describe the workflow correctly.
:::

## Record the computing environment

<div class="environment-stack">
<div><strong>Analysis</strong><span>Your scripts and notebooks</span></div>
<div><strong>Packages</strong><span>pandas &lt;version&gt;, numpy &lt;version&gt;, ...</span></div>
<div><strong>Language</strong><span>Python &lt;version&gt;</span></div>
<div><strong>System</strong><span>Operating system and external tools</span></div>
</div>

Different environments can produce different results.

::: {.notes}
The conceptual requirement is that a future user can reconstruct the relevant
environment. Exact needs depend on the language, tools, and sensitivity of the
analysis.
:::

## Python example: give each project its own virtual environment

```text
Python installation
├── Project A/.venv/ → Project A's Python and packages
└── Project B/.venv/ → Project B's separate Python and packages
```

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

- Activating `.venv` makes its Python and packages current in the terminal
- Packages installed in Project A's environment do not change Project B's
- `.venv/` is a local directory. Add it to `.gitignore`

::: {.notes}
`python -m venv .venv` creates a virtual environment named `.venv` inside the
project. The activation command shown is for macOS and Unix-style shells.
Windows uses a different activation path.

The virtual environment isolates installed packages. It does not tell another
researcher which packages to install. The project must also record the
dependencies and versions.
:::

## Commit the environment recipe, not `.venv/`

```text
research-project/
├── .venv/             local installed environment (ignore)
├── requirements.txt   pinned packages and versions (commit)
└── code/
```

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

A pinned dependency file helps another researcher recreate `.venv/`.

::: {.notes}
A dependency file states what the project requires. A lock file or equivalent
record states the exact versions selected. `requirements.txt` can record exact versions, including transitive
dependencies. Other Python tools use `pyproject.toml` and lock files.

Both isolation and version recording are standard parts of a reproducible
workflow. The specific files depend on the language and package manager.

Version pinning improves repeatability but does not guarantee indefinite
reproduction. Systems, external services, and unavailable packages can still
change.

Sources: [Python virtual environment documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)
and [pip repeatable installs](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/repeatable-installs/).
:::

## Control randomness

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1433)
sample_indices = rng.choice(1000, size=500, replace=True)
```

- Set and record a seed
- Use the same random-number generator
- Document intentional variation across runs

::: {.notes}
A seed fixes the initial state of a pseudorandom number generator. The same
seed can reproduce a sequence when the generator and relevant software remain
the same.

A seed does not correct a flawed simulation or guarantee identical results
across all software and hardware. It removes one avoidable source of variation.
:::

## Language-model API calls can change the analysis input

```text
Input text → prompt + model call → cleaned or coded data → analysis
```

| Source of change | What to record |
|---|---|
| Generated responses can vary across calls | Retain the exact responses used, subject to data permissions |
| A provider can update a model | Record the model ID, date, and available version details |
| A prompt or setting can change | Version the prompt, parameters, and transformation code |

::: {.notes}
This is a preview of the later lecture on AI use. A random seed alone may not
make a remote model call repeatable. A model name may also refer to a service
that changes over time. Treat the response used in the analysis as an input
that must be retained when permissions allow.

This is a reproducibility risk, like an unrecorded random seed or package version.
:::

## Write run instructions in the README

The README should state:

- What the project does and where its inputs come from
- Which environment to create
- Which command runs the analysis
- Where to find the outputs and how to interpret them

For example: from the repository root, run `bash run.sh`.

::: {.notes}
A README is the first guide for a person who did not create the project. It
helps the user understand the purpose, setup, and expected outputs. It should
point to the command that runs the analysis. That command should run a script,
not require the user to copy commands from the README one at a time.
:::

## Summary: keep a clear path from research question to result

| Practice | Why it matters to another person and to your future self |
|---|---|
| Use the command line | Start the project in a known directory and run a documented workflow |
| Use Git | Identify the code for each result and preserve research decisions |
| Script and document the workflow | Identify inputs, recreate the environment, and rerun the result |

::: {.notes}
Return to the motivating audience: someone else may need to reproduce a result,
and your future self will eventually be that person. The command line provides
a repeatable way to enter the project and run one documented workflow. Git
preserves code history and supports safe exploration. The reproducible workflow
records the inputs, environment, settings, and instructions needed to recreate
the result. Together, these practices make research easier to inspect, resume,
and verify.
:::
